s: E. Race-conscious policies, remedies and other classifications.
All racial classifications get strict scrutiny, whether "benign" or invidious and whether federal, state or local (Richmond v. J.A. Croson, 1989; Adarand Constructors v. Peña, 1995).
Remedial programs require a strong basis in evidence of specific identified discrimination by the government unit.
Societal discrimination does not suffice.
Higher education.
Bakke (1978) and Grutter v. Bollinger (2003) permitted race as a "plus" factor for diversity.

Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard (2023) held that Harvard's and UNC's programs fail strict scrutiny: they lacked measurable objectives, used race negatively and as a stereotype, and had no logical end point.
Applicants may still discuss how race affected their lives, so long as the institution treats each as an individual.
K-12 assignment.
Parents Involved (2007) struck racial balancing in student assignment.
Districting.
Race may not predominate in drawing districts without satisfying strict scrutiny (Shaw v. Reno, 1993; Miller v. Johnson, 1995).
Compliance with Voting Rights Act § 2 has been assumed to be a compelling interest (Allen v. Milligan, 2023, applying Gingles). § 2 litigation is evolving; check the current Term.
Sexual orientation.
The Court has not designated it a suspect class.
Rights claims have succeeded under due process combined with equal protection (Lawrence, 2003; Obergefell, 2015).
Race-conscious government action (Croson / Adarand / SFFA).
Is there a racial classification, facial or purposeful?
If so, strict scrutiny applies regardless of motive.
Compelling interest: remedying identified past discrimination by this actor, with a strong evidentiary basis.
Diversity interests must be measurable.
Narrow tailoring: race-neutral alternatives considered; limited duration; no quotas; race never used as a negative or a stereotype.
Is there a logical end point?
